wikitext.*: {{short description|International standard for three-letter codes identifying languages}} {{use dmy dates|date=October 2024}} '''ISO 639-3:2007''', '''''Codes for the representation of names of languages – Part 3: Alpha-3 code for comprehensive coverage of languages''''', is an international standard for [[language code]]s in the [[ISO 639]] series. It defines three-letter codes for identifying languages. The standard was published by [[International Organization for Standardization]] (ISO) on 1 February 2007.{{Cite web |title=ISO 639-3:2007 withdrawn notice |url=https://www.iso.org/standard/39534.html |publisher=International Organization for Standardization |date=1 February 2007 |access-date=6 June 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240606000000/https://www.iso.org/standard/39534.html |archive-date=6 June 2024 |url-status=live}} As of 2023, this edition of the standard has been officially withdrawn and replaced by ISO 639:2023. ISO 639-3 extends the [[ISO 639-2]] alpha-3 codes with an aim to cover all known [[natural language]]s. The extended language coverage was based primarily on the language codes used in the ''[[Ethnologue]]'' (volumes 10–14) published by [[SIL International]], which is now the [[registration authority]] for ISO 639-3.{{Cite web |title=Maintenance agencies and registration authorities |url=http://www.iso.org/iso/home/standards_development/list_of_iso_technical_committees/maintenance_agencies.htm |publisher=ISO |access-date=12 January 2014 |archive-date=8 October 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121008180204/http://www.iso.org/iso/home/standards_development/list_of_iso_technical_committees/maintenance_agencies.htm |url-status=live }} It provides an enumeration of languages as complete as possible, including living and extinct, ancient and constructed, major and minor, written and unwritten. However, it does not include [[reconstructed language]]s such as [[Proto-Indo-European language|Proto-Indo-European]].{{Cite web |title=Types of individual languages – Ancient languages |url=https://iso639-3.sil.org/about/types#Ancient |access-date=2018-06-11 |website=SIL International |archive-date=12 June 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180612140613/https://iso639-3.sil.org/about/types#Ancient |url-status=live }} ISO 639-3 is intended for use as [[metadata]] codes in a wide range of applications. It is widely used in computer and information systems, such as the Internet, in which many languages need to be supported. In archives and other information storage, it is used in cataloging systems, indicating what language a resource is in or about. The codes are also frequently used in the linguistic literature and elsewhere to compensate for the fact that language names may be obscure or ambiguous. {| class="wikitable" width="25%" align="right" ! Find a language |- | style="text-align:center" | Enter an ISO 639-3 code to find the corresponding language article. |- | type=search width=10 default=ISO 639: buttonlabel=Go searchbuttonlabel=Search break=no |} == Language codes == {{main article|List of ISO 639-3 codes}} ISO 639-3 includes all languages in [[ISO 639-1]] and all individual languages in [[ISO 639-2]]. ISO 639-1 and ISO 639-2 focused on major languages, most frequently represented in the total body of the world's literature. Since ISO 639-2 also includes language collections and Part 3 does not, ISO 639-3 is not a superset of ISO 639-2. [[Machine-readable data]] files are provided by the registration authority. Mappings from ISO 639-1 or ISO 639-2 to ISO 639-3 can be done using these data files. ISO 639-3 is intended to assume distinctions based on criteria that are not entirely objective.{{Cite web |title=Scope of Denotation: Individual Languages |url=http://www-01.sil.org/iso639-3/scope.asp#I |website=SIL International |access-date=18 May 2014 |archive-date=20 October 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141020022923/http://www-01.sil.org/iso639-3/scope.asp#I |url-status=live }} It is not intended to document or provide identifiers for dialects or other sub-language variations.{{Cite web |title=Scope of Denotation: Dialects |url=http://www-01.sil.org/iso639-3/scope.asp#Dialects |website=SIL International |access-date=18 May 2014 |archive-date=20 October 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141020022923/http://www-01.sil.org/iso639-3/scope.asp#Dialects |url-status=live }} Nevertheless, judgments regarding distinctions between languages may be subjective, particularly in the case of language varieties without established literary traditions, usage in education or media, or other factors that contribute to language conventionalization. Therefore, the standard should not be regarded as an authoritative statement of what distinct languages exist in the world (about which there may be substantial disagreement in some cases), but rather simply one useful way for identifying different language varieties precisely. == Code space == Since the code is three-letter alphabetic, one upper bound for the number of languages that can be represented is 26 × 26 × 26 = 17,576. Since ISO 639-2 defines special codes (4), a reserved range (520) and [[ISO 639-2#B_and_T_codes|B-only codes]] (22), 546 codes cannot be used in part 3. Therefore, a stricter upper bound is 17,576 − 546 = 17,030. The upper bound gets even stricter if one subtracts the language collections defined in 639-2 and the ones yet to be defined in [[ISO 639-5]]. == Reference names == Reference names may only use a subset of ASCII characters. According to section 6.4.1 of the standard, they may only contain the 26 letters of the [[ISO basic Latin alphabet]] and diacritics from the following set: {{pbl| á é í ó ú â ê î ô û à è ì ò ù ä ë ï ö ü ã ñ õ å ç }} Reference names may also include any of five ASCII punctuation marks (space, hyphen-minus, apostrophe and the parentheses), and within parentheses the full stop and the ten digits. Alternative names may use proper language orthography, if Latin, or transliteration into Latin script that contains additional characters. == Macrolanguages == {{Main article|ISO 639 macrolanguage}} There are 58 languages in ISO 639-2 which are considered, for the purposes of the standard, to be "macrolanguages" in ISO 639-3.{{Cite web |title=Scope of denotation: Macrolanguages |url=http://www.sil.org/iso639-3/scope.asp#M |access-date=2012-06-14 |website=SIL International |archive-date=8 February 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130208184504/http://www.sil.org/iso639-3/scope.asp#M |url-status=live }} Some of these [[macrolanguage]]s had no individual language as defined by ISO 639-3 in the code set of ISO 639-2, e.g. ara (Generic Arabic). Others like nor (Norwegian) had their two individual parts (nno ([[Nynorsk]]), nob ([[Bokmål]])) already in ISO 639-2. That means some languages (e.g. arb, Standard Arabic) that were considered by ISO 639-2 to be dialects of one language (ara) are now in ISO 639-3 in certain contexts considered to be individual languages themselves. This is an attempt to deal with varieties that may be linguistically distinct from each other, but are treated by their speakers as two forms of the same language, e.g. in cases of [[diglossia]]. For example: * ara[https://iso639-3.sil.org/code/ara ara] in the ISO 639-3 registry. (Generic Arabic, 639-2) * arb[https://iso639-3.sil.org/code/arb arb] in the ISO 639-3 registry. (Standard Arabic, 639-3) A complete list is available on the ISO 639-3 registrar's website.{{Cite web |title=Macrolanguage Mappings |url=https://iso639-3.sil.org/code_tables/macrolanguage_mappings/data |access-date=2021-11-02 |website=SIL International |archive-date=11 October 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201011115707/https://iso639-3.sil.org/code_tables/macrolanguage_mappings/data |url-status=live }} == Collective languages == {{See also|ISO 639-2#Collective language codes|ISO 639-5}} "A collective language code element is an identifier that represents a group of individual languages that are not deemed to be one language in any usage context."{{Cite web |title=Scope of denotation: Collective languages |url=http://www.sil.org/iso639-3/scope.asp#C |access-date=2012-06-14 |website=SIL International |archive-date=8 February 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130208184504/http://www.sil.org/iso639-3/scope.asp#C |url-status=live }} These codes do not precisely represent a particular language or macrolanguage. While ISO 639-2 includes three-letter identifiers for collective languages, these codes are excluded from ISO 639-3. Hence ISO 639-3 is not a superset of ISO 639-2. [[ISO 639-5]] defines 3-letter collective codes for language families and groups, including the collective language codes from ISO 639-2. ==Special codes== Four codes are set aside in [[ISO 639-2#Special situations|ISO 639-2]] and ISO 639-3 for cases where none of the specific codes are appropriate. These are intended primarily for applications like databases where an ISO code is required regardless of whether one exists. * {{code|mis}} (uncoded languages, originally an abbreviation for 'miscellaneous') is intended for languages which have not (yet) been included in the ISO standard. * {{code|mul}} (multiple languages) is intended for cases where the data includes more than one language, and (for example) the database requires a single ISO code. * {{code|und}} (undetermined) is intended for cases where the language in the data has not been identified, such as when it is mislabeled or never had been labeled. It is not intended for cases such as [[Trojan language|Trojan]] where an unattested language has been given a name. * {{code|zxx}} (no linguistic content / not applicable) is intended for data which is not a language at all, such as animal calls.{{Cite web |title=Field Recordings of Vervet Monkey Calls |url=https://catalog.ldc.upenn.edu/LDC2004S12 |access-date=2023-01-15 |website=[[Linguistic Data Consortium]] |archive-date=15 January 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230115182534/https://catalog.ldc.upenn.edu/LDC2004S12 |url-status=live }} In addition, 520 codes in the range {{code|qaa}}–{{code|qtz}} are 'reserved for local use'. For example, Rebecca Bettencourt assigns a code to [[constructed language]]s, and new assignments are made upon request.{{Cite web |last=Bettencourt |first=Rebecca |title=ConLang Code Registry |url=https://www.kreativekorp.com/clcr/ |access-date=2021-03-12 |website=KreativeKorp |archive-date=8 October 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231008102538/https://www.kreativekorp.com/clcr/ |url-status=live }} ==Maintenance processes== The code table for ISO 639-3 is open to changes. In order to protect stability of existing usage, the changes permitted are limited to:{{Cite web |title=Submitting ISO 639-3 Change Requests: Types of Changes |url=http://www-01.sil.org/iso639-3/submit_changes.asp#Types |website=SIL International |access-date=21 May 2014 |archive-date=2 February 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160202224243/http://www-01.sil.org/iso639-3/submit_changes.asp#Types |url-status=live }} *modifications to the reference information for an entry (including names or categorizations for type and scope), *addition of new entries, *deprecation of entries that are duplicates or spurious, *merging one or more entries into another entry, and *splitting an existing language entry into multiple new language entries. The code assigned to a language is not changed unless there is also a change in denotation. Changes are made according to an annual cycle. Every request is given a minimum period of three months for public review. The ISO 639-3 Web site has pages that describe "scopes of denotation"{{Cite web |title=Scope of Denotation for Language Identifiers |url=http://www-01.sil.org/iso639-3/scope.asp |website=SIL International |access-date=18 May 2014 |archive-date=20 October 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141020022923/http://www-01.sil.org/iso639-3/scope.asp |url-status=live }} ([[wikt:languoid|languoid]] types) and types of languages,{{Cite web |title=Types of Languages |url=http://www-01.sil.org/iso639-3/types.asp |website=SIL International |access-date=21 May 2014 |archive-date=23 February 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160223002431/http://www-01.sil.org/iso639-3/types.asp |url-status=live }} which explain what concepts are in scope for encoding and certain criteria that need to be met. For example, constructed languages can be encoded, but only if they are designed for human communication and have a body of literature, preventing requests for idiosyncratic inventions. The registration authority documents on its Web site instructions made in the text of the ISO 639-3 standard regarding how the code tables are to be maintained.{{Cite web |title=ISO 639-3 Change Management |url=http://www-01.sil.org/iso639-3/changes.asp |website=SIL International |access-date=18 May 2014 |archive-date=14 May 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160514203537/http://www-01.sil.org/iso639-3/changes.asp |url-status=live }} It also documents the processes used for receiving and processing change requests.{{Cite web |title=Submitting ISO 639-3 Change Requests |url=http://www-01.sil.org/iso639-3/submit_changes.asp |website=SIL International |access-date=21 May 2014 |archive-date=2 February 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160202224243/http://www-01.sil.org/iso639-3/submit_changes.asp |url-status=live }} A change request form is provided, and there is a second form for collecting information about proposed additions. Any party can submit change requests. When submitted, requests are initially reviewed by the registration authority for completeness. When a fully documented request is received, it is added to a published Change Request Index. Also, announcements are sent to the general LINGUIST discussion list at Linguist List and other lists the registration authority may consider relevant, inviting public review and input on the requested change. Any list owner or individual is able to request notifications of change requests for particular regions or language families. Comments that are received are published for other parties to review. Based on consensus in comments received, a change request may be withdrawn or promoted to "candidate status". Three months prior to the end of an annual review cycle (typically in September), an announcement is sent to the LINGUIST discussion list and other lists regarding Candidate Status Change Requests. All requests remain open for review and comment through the end of the annual review cycle. Decisions are announced at the end of the annual review cycle (typically in January). At that time, requests may be adopted in whole or in part, amended and carried forward into the next review cycle, or rejected. Rejections often include suggestions on how to modify proposals for resubmission. A public archive of every change request is maintained along with the decisions taken and the rationale for the decisions.{{Cite web |title=ISO 639-3 Change Request Index |url=http://www-01.sil.org/iso639-3/chg_requests.asp |website=SIL International |access-date=20 May 2014 |archive-date=29 January 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160129022132/http://www-01.sil.org/iso639-3/chg_requests.asp |url-status=live }} ==Criticism== Linguists Morey, Post and Friedman raise various criticisms of ISO 639, and in particular ISO 639-3:{{Cite conference |last1=Morey |first1=Stephen |last2=Post |first2=Mark W. |last3=Friedman |first3=Victor A. |year=2013 |title=The language codes of ISO 639: A premature, ultimately unobtainable, and possibly damaging standardization |url=http://prijipati.library.usyd.edu.au/handle/2123/9838 |conference=PARADISEC RRR Conference |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160223010953/http://prijipati.library.usyd.edu.au/handle/2123/9838 |archive-date=2016-02-23 |access-date=2015-11-03 |url-status=dead}} *The three-letter codes themselves are problematic, because while officially arbitrary technical labels, they are often derived from mnemonic abbreviations for language names, some of which are pejorative. For example, [[Yemsa language|Yemsa]] was assigned the code jnj, from pejorative "Janejero". These codes may thus be considered offensive by native speakers. *The administration of the standard is problematic because SIL is a missionary organization with inadequate transparency and accountability. Decisions as to what deserves to be encoded as a language are made internally. While outside input may or may not be welcomed, the decisions themselves are opaque, and many linguists have given up trying to improve the standard. *Permanent identification of a language is incompatible with language change. *Languages and dialects often cannot be rigorously distinguished, and [[dialect continuum|dialect continua]] may be subdivided in many ways, whereas the standard privileges one choice. Such distinctions are often based instead on social and political factors. *ISO 639-3 may be misunderstood and misused by authorities that make decisions about people's identity and language, abolishing the right of speakers to identify or not to identify with their speech variety. Though SIL is sensitive to such issues, this problem is inherent in the nature of an established standard, which may be used (or mis-used) in ways that ISO and SIL do not intend. [[Martin Haspelmath]] agrees with four of these points, but not the point about language change. He disagrees because any account of a language requires identifying it, and we can easily identify different stages of a language. He suggests that linguists may prefer to use a codification that is made at the [[wikt:languoid|languoid]] level since "it rarely matters to linguists whether what they are talking about is a language, a dialect or a close-knit family of languages." He also questions whether an ISO standard for language identification is appropriate since ISO is an industrial organization, while he views language documentation and nomenclature as a scientific endeavor. He cites the original need for standardized language identifiers as having been "the economic significance of translation and [[Language localisation|software localization]]", for which purposes the ISO 639-1 and 639-2 standards were established. But he raises doubts about industry need for the comprehensive coverage provided by ISO 639-3, including as it does "little-known languages of small communities that are never or hardly used in writing and that are often in danger of extinction".{{Cite web |last=Haspelmath |first=Martin |date=4 December 2013 |title=Can language identity be standardized? On Morey et al.'s critique of ISO 639-3 |url=http://dlc.hypotheses.org/610 |website=Diversity Linguistics Comment |doi=10.58079/nsst |access-date=18 April 2014 |archive-date=19 April 2014
